name: Pompeii
info: Pompeii was a city on the Bay of Naples in Campania, Italy, settled by Oscans in the 8th century BCE, ruled in turn by Etruscans, Samnites and Romans, and buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE.

facts.founded: The first stable settlements on the site date to the 8th century BCE, when the Oscans, a population of central Italy, founded five villages in the area.
facts.where: On a coastal lava plateau about 40 m above sea level, 8 km from Mount Vesuvius and beside the mouth of the Sarno river, near Naples in the Campania region of Italy.
facts.known: Burial under volcanic ash and pumice in 79 CE; Oscan, Greek, Etruscan, Samnite and Roman rule; siege by Sulla in 89 BCE; the earthquake of 62 CE; wine and oil trade; graffiti in colloquial Latin; plaster casts of the dead
facts.today: The ruins lie in the municipality of Pompei and form a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

t: Pompeii grew from Oscan villages of the 8th century BCE into a walled town that passed under Greek, Etruscan, Samnite and then Roman influence, and became a Roman colony after Sulla besieged it in 89 BCE.
A severe earthquake struck on 5 February 62, and the town was still being rebuilt when the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 buried it under ash and pumice.
The ruins stayed largely undisturbed until the late 16th century, and excavation since the mid-18th century has made Pompeii a main source for the study of Roman life and urban planning.
dyk: Giuseppe Fiorelli realised in 1863 that voids in the ash were spaces left by decomposed bodies, and devised the technique of injecting plaster into them to recreate the forms of the victims.
ev: The Oscans found five villages on the site
Cumae, allied with Syracuse, defeats the Etruscans and gains control of the area
Sulla besieges Pompeii, which becomes a Roman colony
The Amphitheatre of Pompeii is built
A severe earthquake damages the city
Mount Vesuvius erupts and buries Pompeii
Giuseppe Fiorelli takes charge and introduces plaster casts and scientific documentation

sections.origins:
Pompeii was built about 40 m above sea level on a coastal lava plateau formed by earlier eruptions of Mount Vesuvius, 8 km away. The plateau fell steeply to the south and partly to the west into the sea. The city once stood by the shoreline and is today about 700 m inland. The mouth of the navigable Sarno river, beside the city, was protected by lagoons and served early Greek and Phoenician sailors as a haven port, which the Romans later developed. According to Theodor Kraus, the name may come from the Oscan word for the number five, pompe, which would suggest that the community consisted of five hamlets, or that it was settled by a family group, the gens Pompeia.

The first stable settlements on the site date to the 8th century BCE, when the Oscans, a population of central Italy, founded five villages in the area. From around 740 BCE the Greeks arrived in Campania and Pompeii entered their orbit. The Doric Temple, the most important building of this period, stood away from the centre, in what later became the Triangular Forum, and the cult of Apollo was introduced. In the early 6th century BCE the villages merged into a single community at the crossroad between Cumae, Nola and Stabiae, surrounded by a tufa wall that enclosed much more than the early town, including agricultural land. A small port was built near the river mouth.
sections.growth:
The city grew in stages. Its earliest part lay in regions VII and VIII, with an irregular street plan, and expansion from this old town accelerated after 450 BCE. In the late 4th century BCE the city began to spread from its nucleus into the open area inside the walls, with a more regular street plan. The walls were reinforced in the early 3rd century BCE, and again after the outbreak of the Second Punic War in 218 BCE, when Hannibal's invasion threatened many cities. Pompeii continued to flourish through the production and trade of wine and oil with places such as Provence and Spain, and through intensive agriculture on farms around the city.

In the 2nd century BCE it enriched itself by taking part in Rome's conquest of the east. A statue of Apollo in the Forum was erected by Lucius Mummius in gratitude for the city's support in the sack of Corinth. These riches let Pompeii expand to its ultimate limits, and the Forum and many public and private buildings were built, among them the Large Theatre, the Temple of Jupiter, the Basilica, the Stabian Baths and a two-storey portico. By the time of Sulla's conquest in 89 BCE the street layout was largely complete and most of the insulae were built. The city covered 64 to 67 hectares. Its population in 79 CE is put at 20,000 by one estimate, while household counts give 11,000 to 11,500.
sections.rulers:
By 524 BCE the Etruscans had settled in the area, including Pompeii, which became a member of the Etruscan League of cities. Like the Greeks, they controlled the city without conquering it militarily, and Pompeii enjoyed a sort of autonomy. In 474 BCE Cumae, allied with Syracuse, defeated the Etruscans at the Battle of Cumae and gained control of the area. The Samnites, a people from Abruzzo and Molise and allies of the Romans, conquered Greek Cumae between 423 and 420 BCE, and it is likely that the surrounding territory, Pompeii included, had been conquered around 424 BCE. The new rulers gradually imposed their architecture and enlarged the town.

From 343 BCE the Samnite Wars brought a Roman army into the Campanian plain. Although governed by the Samnites, Pompeii entered the Roman orbit and stayed faithful to Rome through the third Samnite war and the war against Pyrrhus. After the Samnite Wars, from 290 BCE, it had to accept the status of socii of Rome, keeping its own language and administration. Pompeii rebelled in the Social Wars, and in 89 BCE Sulla besieged it. It surrendered after the conquest of Nola and became a Roman colony named Colonia Cornelia Veneria Pompeianorum. Sulla's veterans were given land and property, many who had opposed Rome were dispossessed, and the Pompeians were granted Roman citizenship.
sections.life:
After the conquest Latin became the main language of the city, and many old aristocratic families Latinised their names as a sign of assimilation. The graffiti on outside walls and inside rooms give many examples of the colloquial Vulgar Latin spoken at the time, in contrast to the formal language of classical writers. Excavation has uncovered hundreds of private homes and businesses reflecting various architectural styles and social classes, and luxurious houses with lavish decoration. Among them are the House of the Faun, the House of the Vettii and the House of Menander, and outside the walls the Villa of the Mysteries.

The public buildings included the Forum, two theatres, at least four public baths and the Amphitheatre, which scholars have cited as a model of crowd control. An aqueduct, a branch of the Serino Aqueduct, supplied the public baths, more than 25 street fountains and many private houses and businesses. There were at least 31 bakeries, nearly 100 thermopolia that sold hot food and drink, and workshops for wool, among them fulleries and the Building of Eumachia, which was the wool market or the seat of the fullers' guild. A garum workshop made fish sauce. Wine was exported, and barley, wheat, millet and olive oil were also produced. Carbonised remains show that people ate emmer wheat, chickpeas, figs, olives, grapes, walnuts and many other plants.
sections.crises:
Sulla's siege of 89 BCE left its traces in the walls. He targeted the vulnerable Porta Ercolano with artillery, and the impact craters of thousands of ballista shots can still be seen. Many nearby buildings inside the walls were destroyed. In 59 CE a serious riot and bloodshed in the amphitheatre between Pompeians and Nucerians, recorded in a fresco, led the Roman Senate to send the Praetorian Guard and to ban further events for ten years.

On 5 February 62 a severe earthquake did considerable damage around the bay, particularly to Pompeii, and is believed to have registered between 5 and 6 on the Richter scale. Fires caused by fallen oil lamps added to the panic. Between 62 and 79 most rebuilding was done in the private sector, and some public buildings, such as the Central Baths, were begun after the earthquake. The city was still flourishing.

In 79 CE Mount Vesuvius erupted, in one of the deadliest eruptions in history, which lasted two days. A rain of pumice lasted about 18 hours and allowed most inhabitants to escape; only about 1,150 bodies have been found on the site. Then pyroclastic flows struck, incinerating or suffocating those who remained. A study published in 2010 indicates that heat was the main cause of death. Pliny the Younger described the eruption from Misenum; his uncle Pliny the Elder died trying to rescue victims. The date is disputed: one version of Pliny's letter gives August, another as late as 23 November, a charcoal inscription found in 2018 gives 17 October, and a study of 2022 determined 24 to 25 October.
sections.legacy:
Titus appointed two ex-consuls to organise relief and gave large sums from the imperial treasury, but no work was done on recovery. Survivors and possibly thieves salvaged valuables, and the site was reoccupied as a small informal settlement that lasted until the fifth century. The name and location were forgotten, though Pompeii appears on the Tabula Peutingeriana of the 4th century. Further eruptions in 471 to 473 and in 512 covered the remains more deeply, and the area became known as La Civita.

In 1592 the architect Domenico Fontana ran into painted walls while digging an aqueduct, but kept the find secret. Excavations at the site began in 1748 under Roque Joaquin de Alcubierre, and an inscription found on 20 August 1763 identified the city as Pompeii. Karl Weber directed the first scientific excavations. Under the French, who ruled Italy from 1806 to 1815, up to 700 workers were employed. Giuseppe Fiorelli took charge in 1863, devised the plaster casts and divided the city into nine regiones and its blocks into insulae. In the 1920s Amedeo Maiuri dug below the layers of 79 for the first time, and by 1960 most of Pompeii had been uncovered. The Allied bombing of the Second World War and the earthquake of 1980 caused further damage.

Pompeii is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. About two thirds of the city has been excavated, and work now concentrates on documenting the ruins and slowing their decay, though new areas have been explored since 2018.

summary: Pompeii was a city on the Bay of Naples, founded by Oscans in the 8th century BCE and ruled by Etruscans, Samnites and Romans. Mount Vesuvius buried it in 79 CE. Its ruins, excavated since the mid-18th century, show Roman life.

notes: START: the article dates the first stable settlements to the 8th century BC (Oscan villages); I used -750 with circa true. END 79 is the eruption; the article says a small informal settlement lasted on the site until the fifth century.

POPULATION: the article gives 10,000 to 20,000, 11,000 to 11,500 from household counts (Geography), 'a population of 20,000' by 79 and 'more recent estimates up to 11,500'. These conflict; I stated both without choosing.

ERUPTION DATE is disputed in the article (August, 23 November, 17 October charcoal inscription, 24-25 October by a 2022 study); all given. The article's other evidence for an autumn date was left out for space.
Event '70 BCE' Amphitheatre: the article says 'in 70 BC'. Event '1748': the article says Alcubierre excavated at Pompeii in 1748 'even if the city was not identified'.
'Pompeii was never taken by force at first' in rulers is my phrasing of the article saying the Greeks and Etruscans controlled it without military conquest; reword if the editor finds it too strong.

Battle of Cumae 474 BCE and the Samnite conquest of Cumae 423-420 BCE are as given. The article says 'It is likely that all of the surrounding territory, including Pompeii, was already conquered around 424 BC'; hedged.

Left out as tourism or present-day matters: visitor numbers, ticket limits, the 2010 Schola Armatorum collapse, UNESCO's 2013 warning, popular culture, documentaries, the Antiquarium, recent finds of 2018 to 2024 beyond a general mention, and the erotic art section (the secret cabinet). The article gives the UNESCO listing date as 1997 in one place; not stated here.

The article says the Roman Senate banned events 'for ten years' after the riot of 59 and places the Nero visit in about 64; the latter was left out. 'Heat was the main cause of death' is the 2010 study's finding as the article reports it.
The Etruscan and Greek 'orbit' wording follows the article. Whether the Samnites took Pompeii by conquest is not stated beyond 'likely'.
